items.title: Controllers reconcile state
items.body: Kubernetes is declarative: desired state is stored in the API server, and controllers run control loops that observe actual state and act to close the gap. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, which create or delete Pods until the count matches.
items.question: What happens if you kubectl delete a Pod owned by a Deployment?
items.answer: Its ReplicaSet sees fewer Pods than desired and creates a replacement. To remove it for good, scale down or delete the owning Deployment.

items.title: Liveness probes that cause outages
items.question: Your liveness probe checks the database connection. During a brief database outage every Pod restarts repeatedly, making recovery slower. What went wrong?
items.answer: Failing liveness restarts the container, so it should only detect a process that cannot recover by itself, such as a deadlock. Dependency checks belong in readiness, which removes the Pod from Service endpoints without restarting it. Use a startupProbe for slow boots so liveness does not kill them early.

source.name: Kubernetes docs - Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

items.title: CPU limits and throttling
items.question: Why can a Pod with a CPU limit be slow even when the node has idle CPU?
items.answer: CPU limits are enforced as a quota per scheduling period; once a container uses its quota it is throttled until the next period, regardless of idle capacity. Requests drive scheduling and the proportional share under contention. Memory is different: exceeding a memory limit gets the container OOM-killed.

source.name: Kubernetes docs - Resource Management for Pods and Containers

items.title: Secrets are only base64
items.body: Secret values are base64-encoded in manifests, which is encoding, not encryption. Protect them with RBAC, enable encryption at rest for the API server data, and never commit them to Git unencrypted.

items.title: Errors during rolling deploys
items.question: During rolling deploys, clients see a burst of connection errors. The app exits immediately on SIGTERM. What should change?
items.answer: Endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen concurrently, so load balancers may keep routing to the Pod briefly. Keep serving for a few seconds (a preStop sleep or delayed shutdown), stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight requests, and exit within terminationGracePeriodSeconds.

items.title: Services give stable addresses
items.body: A Service provides a stable virtual IP and a DNS name such as my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster.local, and routes traffic to ready Pods whose labels match its selector. Pods are ephemeral and change IPs, so clients should never address them directly.
